subject: Maths
central_question: How does unique prime factorisation help us analyse integers, compute HCF and LCM, and prove that important real numbers are irrational?
in_scope_units: Introduction: links real numbers with divisibility, prime factorisation, HCF and LCM, and irrational numbers.
The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic: prime factorisation, uniqueness, and applications to divisibility, HCF and LCM.
Revisiting Irrational Numbers: the prime-divisor theorem and proofs by contradiction for square roots and related expressions.
Summary and note to the reader: consolidates the chapter results and distinguishes the two-number HCF-LCM product rule from the three-number case.
banned_topics: A full procedure for Euclid's division algorithm, because no worked section on that algorithm appears in the supplied chapter text.
The theorem classifying terminating and non-terminating recurring decimal expansions, because it is mentioned in the introduction but not developed in the supplied chapter text.
Complex numbers or irrationality proofs involving non-real square roots.
must_include_keywords: HCF(a, b) × LCM(a, b) = a × b

known_pitfalls.claim: A composite number can have two genuinely different prime factorisations.
known_pitfalls.correction: By the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, its prime factorisation is unique apart from the order of the prime factors.

known_pitfalls.claim: For HCF, take the greatest power of every prime appearing in either number.
known_pitfalls.correction: For HCF, take the smallest power of each common prime factor; the greatest powers of all involved primes are used for the LCM.

known_pitfalls.claim: HCF × LCM equals the product of the numbers for any number of integers.
known_pitfalls.correction: The identity HCF(a, b) × LCM(a, b) = a × b is stated for two positive integers; Example 4 shows it does not extend in that simple form to three integers.

known_pitfalls.claim: To prove √p irrational, it is enough to say that p is not a perfect square.
known_pitfalls.correction: The chapter uses proof by contradiction: assume √p = a/b in lowest terms and show that p divides both a and b, contradicting coprimality.

recommended_example_progression: Start with the factor tree of 32760 from Section 1.2 to illustrate prime factorisation and uniqueness.
Use NCERT Example 2 and Example 3 to compute HCF and LCM and verify the two-number product relation.
Use NCERT Example 1 and Exercise 1.1 Question 6 to apply prime factors to last-digit and compositeness arguments.
Use Theorem 1.3 and NCERT Example 5 to model a complete proof by contradiction for √2 and √3.
Finish with NCERT Examples 6 and 7 and Exercise 1.2 to prove irrationality of expressions formed from rational and irrational numbers.
ncert_end_of_chapter_exercises_reference: The supplied chapter contains Exercise 1.1 on prime factorisation, HCF and LCM, and Exercise 1.2 on irrationality proofs.
